messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: size(vector_varaible) in function not compiling / extended stan syntax to avoid little helper functs
parts:
Hi!

Maybe I used the size call wrong, but the attached stan model does not compile for me. That is getting the size of a vector in a function does not seem to work.

BTW, functions are great, but I find myself writing stuff like the countPositives int the example in order to make simple declarations possible in the transformed data block like in the stan file. If a syntax like

transformed data {
  vector[sum(someInput>0)] vectorForPositiveStuff;
}

would be possible - that would be great! This may cause a headache for the language processing, but couldn't one possibly define this as lambda functions?

Just a thought. But the more I explore the functions the more I like it!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] size(vector_varaible) in function not compiling / extended stan syntax to avoid little helper functs
parts:
> On Feb 26, 2015, at 12:12 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi!
>
> Maybe I used the size call wrong, but the attached stan model does not compile for me. That is getting the size of a vector in a function does not seem to work.

size() is only defined for arrays. And then
it's just the size of the first dimension.

The num_elements() function should work. Or you
can use rows() or cols().

> BTW, functions are great, but I find myself writing stuff like the countPositives int the example in order to make simple declarations possible in the transformed data block like in the stan file. If a syntax like
>
> transformed data {
> vector[sum(someInput>0)] vectorForPositiveStuff;
> }
>
> would be possible - that would be great!

The inefficient implementation that allocates a new array
and copies to it wouldn't be that hard to implement. But
then we'd want to do it for all the operators, which means
a lot of cases.
> This may cause a headache for the language processing, but couldn't one possibly define this as lambda functions?

The C++ idiom to use to make it efficient would return an
expression template, which is like a lazy lambda function for
the whole value (someInput > 0).

Of course, if we introduced lambda functions into Stan, then
we could do these kinds of things very generally, with this
one being something like:

sum(map(x.(x > 0), someInput))

x.(x > 0) would be a function that returned 1 if its input was > 0
and 0 otherwise. map(function, container) would apply the function
elementwise to the members of the container, creating a new container.
Then sum() is what we already have.

What we really need is some way to test functions, though I
believe Jiqiang has workable solution for R.

- Bob

parts:
Hi Bob!

Thanks. Maybe the documentation then needs an update? Quote from page 318:

"The size() function extracts the number of elements in an array. The function is
overloaded to apply to arrays of integers, reals, matrices, vectors, and row vectors."

To confirm: The num_elements function works.

If lambdas are possible without too much hassle, then I would strongly support this. Lambda expressions gave me quite a headache in the first place to understand how they work and how I get the syntax right, but once I got that, I started to use them all over the place. Just so useful!

Best,
Sebastian
